projects.title: ACT Farm
projects.summary: A regenerative agriculture and creative practice project grounded in therapeutic landscapes — growing food, community, and connection to country.
projects.overview: ACT Farm is the studio practice — the operational heart where methodology becomes action. It's where ACT prototypes, learns, fails, iterates, and prepares tools for handover. Located on Jinibara Country near Witta, Queensland, it sits within the same land as Black Cockatoo Valley and works in partnership with The Harvest in Witta town. The farm serves as: - Living laboratory for regenerative innovation - Studio space where land practice meets technology - Prototype ground for tools and processes - Training base for community capability building - Home for the work that matters

projects.title: ACT Public Voice
projects.summary: How A Curious Tractor describes itself to the world — in the words chosen for act.place.

projects.title: ACT Regenerative Studio
projects.summary: Central hub and coordination point for the entire ACT ecosystem. Where technology serves community ownership.
projects.overview: The ACT Regenerative Studio is the public-facing website and central infrastructure hub at act.place. It is not just a website — it is the coordination layer that connects all ecosystem projects, manages contacts, holds the living knowledge base (Compendium), and provides the administrative backbone for ACT's operations. It sits on the shared ACT Supabase instance (tednluwflfhxyucgwigh), which serves the Command Center, the Telegram bot, GrantScope, and most ACT scripts.

projects.title: Barkly Backbone
projects.summary: A backbone organisation doesn't do the work — it makes the work possible. In the Barkly, that distinction is the difference between communities thriving and communities burning out.
projects.overview: Barkly Backbone is an early-stage concept for a shared operational infrastructure serving community organisations in the Barkly region of the Northern Territory. The Barkly — centred on Tennant Creek, approximately 500km north of Alice Springs — is one of Australia's most remote and geographically dispersed regions, with a predominantly Aboriginal population spread across vast distances and served by a small number of chronically under-resourced organisations. The concept draws from the "backbone organisation" model developed in collective impact theory: a dedicated entity that provides shared services — administration, technology, data, logistics, governance support — so that frontline community organisations don't have to build those capabilities themselves. Every hour a Tennant Creek youth worker spends on compliance paperwork is an hour not spent with a young person. Barkly Backbone is the concept that addresses that equation.

projects.title: BG Fit
projects.summary: A culturally grounded fitness, healing, and mentorship program addressing the overrepresentation of Indigenous youth in the justice system — using movement and country to disrupt the punitive cycle.
projects.overview: BG Fit operates in Mount Isa and Doomadgee, communities where Indigenous youth face disproportionate contact with the justice system. The program works from a premise that physical fitness, cultural connection, and Elder mentorship — not punishment — are the most effective interventions. By grounding health and wellbeing in culture and country, BG Fit creates conditions for young people to build identity, purpose, and community belonging. The results are striking: participating youth have reduced their average police contact from approximately 5 incidents per year to less than 1.

projects.title: Black Cockatoo Valley
projects.summary: Conservation-first. We work with Country, not on it. The land sets the pace; we do not scale beyond what the land and community can carry.
projects.overview: Black Cockatoo Valley is a 150-acre property on Jinibara Country near Witta, Queensland. It is the land holding that grounds ACT's entire physical practice — the site where residencies, R&D, habitat restoration, and community programs take place. Together with The Harvest (the former nursery in Witta town), Black Cockatoo Valley forms ACT's "Place" cluster — the land base that makes all the digital and social enterprise work legible.

projects.title: CAMPFIRE
projects.summary: A cultural immersion, fitness, and mentorship program for Indigenous youth in Mount Isa and surrounding communities, founded by Brodie Germaine.
projects.overview: CAMPFIRE is not just a program — it is a passage. Founded by Brodie Germaine, a Pitta Pitta and Wakka Wakka man from Kalkadoon Country in Mount Isa, CAMPFIRE integrates cultural reconnection to Country, physical fitness, and mentorship to interrupt the cycles of youth crime and disconnection that plague Northwest Queensland. The program's name reflects both method and metaphor: the campfire as a gathering place where stories are shared, wisdom is passed down, and communities remember who they are. It stands as a counter-narrative to the dominant response — approximately $1 million per year to keep a single young person in youth detention — arguing instead that transformation happens through belonging, not punishment.

projects.title: Caring for Those Who Care
projects.summary: A sector sustainability initiative identifying and filling the wellbeing gaps for NFP leaders and workers — research-led, storytelling-powered, and grounded in the conviction that sustaining the carers is inseparable from sustaining the communities they serve.
projects.overview: Caring for Those Who Care addresses a structural blind spot in the social sector: the people who dedicate their working lives to holding communities together are themselves underserved, under-supported, and often operating at significant personal cost. NFP leaders in particular carry a particular burden — responsible for organisations, staff, and communities, expected to model resilience, and often without the peer support or institutional backing that leaders in other sectors take for granted. The project combines rigorous research, community storytelling, and practical recommendations to identify the gaps and build the case for systemic change in how the sector cares for its own.

projects.title: Cars and Microcontrollers
projects.summary: Making things with your hands is not a hobby. For some young people, it's the first time their intelligence has been recognised.
projects.overview: Cars and Microcontrollers is an ACT project at the intersection of maker culture, electronics, and hands-on learning. The project puts young people in contact with physical machines — cars, engines, circuits, microcontrollers — and treats the work of understanding and building those machines as a legitimate site of learning, identity, and creative practice. The Notion project record confirms status as Active (as of February 2026). Operational detail in the wiki is thin — this project has not yet had its full source material ingested. What follows frames Cars and Microcontrollers within the ACT ecosystem and its underlying logic, based on confirmed status and ecosystem positioning.

projects.title: CivicGraph
projects.summary: 587,390 entities connected by 1,535,772 relationships across 254 tables and 29.5M records. Making government spending, influence, and outcomes visible.
projects.overview: CivicGraph is ACT's civic transparency platform. It connects public data to make government spending, influence, and outcomes visible. Every claim is traceable to data. It is the systemic data layer of The Third Reality and the practical implementation of the Civic World Model.

projects.title: Community Capital
projects.summary: The gap between community organisations doing extraordinary work and the capital that could sustain them is not a knowledge gap. It's a relationship gap.
projects.overview: Community Capital is an ACT-facilitated leadership retreat — formally titled the 10x10 Community Capital Leadership Retreat (confirmed by Notion project sync, February 2026) — bringing together community leaders and social impact capital. It is funded via the Social Impact Hub Foundation, which distributes approximately $10 million in funds to not-for-profits annually. ACT's role is facilitation: creating and holding the space between people doing community-level work and people with access to capital, without imposing its own agenda on either.

projects.title: ConFit Pathways
projects.summary: A fitness and boxing-based youth transformation program using mentors with lived incarceration experience to build pathways out of the justice system.
projects.overview: ConFit Pathways is a community intervention program that uses physical fitness — primarily boxing — as a vehicle for personal transformation among young people in or at risk of entering the justice system. Its distinguishing feature is the deliberate recruitment of mentors who have been through the prison system themselves. This lived-experience model creates relationships based on credibility and genuine understanding, not institutional authority. Founded by Joe Kwon, ConFit operates on a simple principle: the same discipline that builds a fighter can rebuild a life. Through structured training, mentoring, and community connection, it offers young people legitimate pathways to identity, income, and belonging — the things that keep people out of the system.

projects.title: CONTAINED
projects.summary: An experiential design campaign about youth detention — placing people inside the question of what we're actually paying for, and what we could choose instead.
projects.overview: CONTAINED is ACT's immersive advocacy campaign at the intersection of experiential design and youth justice reform. It takes the evidence that sits inside JusticeHub — the dry cost comparisons, the recidivism rates, the funding breakdowns — and transforms it into a felt experience. Something people walk through, not just read about. The central provocation: what if we spent $1.55M on keeping a child connected to family, culture, and community instead of locking them away? CONTAINED isn't a report. It isn't a petition. It's a designed environment that makes the economic and human cost of youth incarceration visceral and undeniable — then leaves people with the evidence that something better is not only possible, but already working.

projects.title: Dad.Lab.25
projects.summary: A community-led men's health initiative supporting fathers through peer connection, culturally appropriate wellbeing programs, and honest inquiry into what it means to be a dad today.
projects.overview: Dad.Lab.25 responds to a recognised gap: men's health challenges — particularly for fathers — are poorly served by mainstream health and community services. The program takes a community-led approach, building peer support networks and culturally appropriate interventions that meet fathers where they are, rather than expecting them to fit into clinical or institutional frameworks. The "25" signals a contemporary, forward-looking orientation — this is not a nostalgic or prescriptive model of fatherhood, but an open inquiry into what fathers need and what communities can offer them.

projects.title: DeadlyLabs
projects.summary: STEM education meets youth detention — where sports science converges with cultural identity to redefine futures.
projects.overview: DeadlyLabs is a project of DeadlyScience, an Indigenous-led initiative founded in 2019 by Corey Tutt (Kamilaroi man) to make STEM education accessible for remote Indigenous communities. The "Kickin' It" program brings sports science into youth detention centres, engaging detained young people as co-creators of STEM kits. The partnership with Acmena Youth Justice Centre allows detained youth to become innovators — infusing their perspectives into STEM kits that celebrate the scientific legacy of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people.

projects.title: Designing for Obsolescence
projects.summary: A core ACT philosophy and manifesto: the most successful social innovation is one that makes the social entrepreneur unnecessary — designing systems that hand power back to communities and then get out of the way.
projects.overview: Designing for Obsolescence is not a program but a governing intellectual framework at the heart of ACT's approach. It argues that the dominant model of social innovation — scaling organisations, building dependency, and measuring success by headcount or revenue — is itself part of the problem. True success means the communities ACT works with no longer need ACT. This framework is a direct critique of what it calls the social innovation industrial complex: a self-perpetuating ecosystem of charities, consultants, and intermediaries whose institutional survival depends on the persistence of the very problems they claim to solve. By centering knowledge transfer and community ownership from the outset, ACT aims to design its own obsolescence into every project it touches.

projects.title: Diagrama
projects.summary: Spain's leading therapeutic detention model as an alternative to Australia's punitive justice system — studying, learning from, and working toward an ethical, Indigenous-led transfer of therapeutic detention knowledge to Australia.
projects.overview: Diagrama refers to ACT's engagement with Fundación Diagrama, a Spanish organisation that has developed one of the world's most respected therapeutic detention models for young people in conflict with the law. Spain's youth justice system, with Diagrama as a central implementing partner, has achieved remarkable outcomes — reduced reoffending, improved mental health, and the genuine rehabilitation of young people — through an approach grounded in therapeutic relationships, dignity, and care rather than punishment and containment. The Foundation was established in 1991 and has spent over 35 years operating youth re-education centres across Spain. In 2002, Diagrama founded the International Juvenile Justice Observatory (IJJO) in Brussels, which provides the research and policy framework for international knowledge transfer. ACT's interest in Diagrama sits within JusticeHub's broader mission: identifying and adapting justice alternatives that could reduce Australia's catastrophic rates of Indigenous incarceration, particularly among young people.

projects.title: Empathy Ledger
projects.summary: Not your story... not my story... but a third reality we can only discover together.
projects.overview: The Empathy Ledger is ACT's sovereign storytelling platform — the narrative sovereignty layer of The Third Reality. It gives marginalized and Indigenous communities cryptographic ownership of their narratives, ensuring stories are never extracted but always owned.

projects.title: Empathy Ledger Annual Field Service
projects.summary: Y1 approach: bespoke engagement at ~$50K/year per org with four existing customers (JCF, PICC, Buttery, SMART Recovery). Learn what each org actually buys, then productise in Y2 based on real patterns.

projects.title: Feel Good Project
projects.summary: A haircut is not a haircut. For a woman who has been invisible for months, it's someone saying: you are worth looking after.
projects.overview: The Feel Good Project is an ACT-supported initiative providing mobile hair care and beauty services to women experiencing hardship — homelessness, domestic violence, poverty, or crisis. ACT's contribution was helping build a caravan: a mobile salon that brings the service to where women are, rather than asking women in difficult circumstances to navigate their way to a fixed location. The project is active. Financial tracking in Xero under ACT-FG — Feel Good Project confirms it has incurred costs. Deeper operational detail — the partner organisation, service geography, and outcomes data — has not yet been fully ingested into the wiki.

projects.title: Fishers Oysters
projects.summary: A cultural-first aquaculture enterprise reclaiming and restoring Moreton Bay's oyster industry through Indigenous knowledge, community ownership, and regenerative practice.
projects.overview: Fishers Oysters is working to restore the oyster industry of Moreton Bay through a framework that places Indigenous knowledge first. The project treats ecological restoration and economic sovereignty as inseparable: the reef cannot be healthy without the cultural knowledge systems that have managed it for generations, and those knowledge systems cannot be sustained without the economic sovereignty that comes from community ownership of the enterprise. The name "Fishers" signals both the people (fishing families and custodians) and the act — this is a project about reclaiming the right to fish, to own, and to steward.

projects.title: Global Laundry Alliance
projects.summary: A dignity-centred international network connecting community laundry hubs — advocating for policy change that recognises clean clothing and access to basic hygiene as a matter of human dignity, not charity.
projects.overview: The Global Laundry Alliance grows from one of the most unexpected and powerful social innovations of recent Australian history: Orange Sky Laundry, co-founded by ACT co-founder Nicholas Marchesi OAM. Orange Sky demonstrated that a mobile laundry service for people experiencing homelessness was not primarily about clean clothes — it was about dignity, belonging, and the five-minute conversation that happened while the washing was on. The Global Laundry Alliance takes that insight international: building a network of organisations running community laundry hubs worldwide, sharing knowledge and practice, and collectively advocating for the policy conditions that make this work sustainable and scalable.

projects.title: Gold.Phone
projects.summary: A random connection voice platform and community installation tackling social isolation through authentic, unscripted human conversation — open-source, privacy-focused, and designed for local replication.
projects.overview: Gold.Phone addresses the social isolation crisis with a deceptively simple intervention: connect two strangers by voice, at random, with no social media profile, no metrics, and no agenda. The platform creates conditions for genuine human connection that algorithmic social networks cannot — and deliberately will not — provide. The project operates as both a digital platform and a physical community installation, making it accessible in contexts where smartphone apps are not the right interface. Its open-source foundation means any community can replicate and own their own version.

projects.title: Goods on Country
projects.summary: Manufacturing durable household goods from 100% recycled plastic for remote and marginalised Australian communities — where conventional products fail within weeks.
projects.overview: Goods on Country is ACT's circular economy social enterprise. It designs, manufactures, and deploys indestructible household goods for remote Aboriginal and marginalised communities across Australia, where extreme heat, overcrowding, dust, and limited repair infrastructure destroy standard products in weeks rather than years. The enterprise operates through A Curious Tractor Pty Ltd (ABN: 21 591 780 066) and trades at goodsoncountry.com.au. It is not an Indigenous-owned organisation — it partners deeply with Indigenous-owned organisations (Oonchiumpa, Wilya Janta) and community bodies. Communities are co-designers, not recipients. Internal project code: ACT-GD

projects.title: GrantScope (CivicGraph)
projects.summary: Decision infrastructure connecting supplier intelligence, place-based funding data, and outcome evidence.
projects.status: Active — Circle One technical reference for [[three-circles|The Three Circles]]

projects.title: Green Harvest Witta
projects.summary: The bones of a nursery that became The Harvest — a specific piece of land, a specific man, and the archaeology of what working country looks like before someone turns it into a scenic drive.

projects.title: June's Patch
projects.summary: A network of therapeutic gardens providing nature prescriptions for Queensland healthcare workers — responding to a mental health crisis in the caring professions through land, community, and evidence-based social prescribing.
projects.overview: June's Patch addresses a hidden crisis: the mental health of the people who care for everyone else. Healthcare workers — nurses, doctors, paramedics, allied health staff — face some of the highest rates of burnout, compassion fatigue, and psychological injury of any workforce. June's Patch responds not with clinical programs or EAP services but with something more fundamental: soil, plants, community, and time. The project creates a network of therapeutic gardens in Queensland, specifically designed as accessible nature prescription sites for healthcare workers. Each garden is a place of refuge, restoration, and reconnection — with nature, with peers, and with a sense of purpose beyond the clinical environment. The name honours the tradition of kitchen and patch gardens as places of care and nourishment — practical, grounded, and rooted in relationship.

projects.title: JusticeHub
projects.summary: Evidence-based justice alternatives — proving what works, routing capital to what heals.
projects.overview: JusticeHub is ACT's evidence platform for justice alternatives. It catalogs community-led programs, tracks their outcomes, and provides the fiduciary evidence needed to divert funds from detention to healing. It is the evidence layer of The Third Reality.

projects.title: Minderoo Pitch Package — STAY (Crescendo tier)
projects.summary: The operational version. Not the prose pitch (that's SHIPPED-2026-04-09-minderoo-stay-pitch.md). This is the package that runs the conversation: who calls Lucy when, with what amount, on what timeline, with what supporting artefacts, and how it connects to the CONTAINED launch ten days from now.
projects.status: ready for Ben's first call action

projects.title: Mounty Yarns
projects.summary: A community storytelling project in Mount Gravatt — gathering and preserving local knowledge through yarning, oral history, and cultural exhibition.
projects.overview: Mounty Yarns is rooted in a simple conviction: that communities hold extraordinary knowledge about themselves, and that preserving and sharing that knowledge is both an act of dignity and a source of community strength. Operating in the Mount Gravatt area of Brisbane, the project uses yarning circles, oral history methods, and community gathering to capture stories that would otherwise be lost. The project operates at the intersection of community memory, cultural identity, and place — holding space for the stories that official histories overlook.

projects.title: Oonchiumpa
projects.summary: Aboriginal-led youth program in Mparntwe (Alice Springs) — grounding young people in culture, Country, and identity across seven language groups of Central Australia.
projects.overview: Oonchiumpa is a 100% Aboriginal-led youth civic agency based in Mparntwe (Alice Springs, NT), working across homeland communities within a 150km radius. The program serves young people from seven language groups — including Arrernte, Alyawarra, Luritja, and Warlpiri — connecting them to Country, culture, and civic agency through mentorship, on-Country healing, and cross-community exchange. The name and program operate under the cultural authority of Aunty Bev and Uncle Terry. The central site is Atnarpa homestead on Loves Creek Station — the Bloomfield family's reclaimed ancestral Country, approximately 80km east of Alice Springs. Oonchiumpa is one of ACT's two primary community partnerships alongside Palm Island Community Company (PICC). It is also a key proof point within JusticeHub for the effectiveness of community-led alternatives to youth detention.

projects.title: Palm Island Community Company (PICC)
projects.summary: A pioneering case study in community control — from state-managed settlement to 100% Aboriginal Community Controlled Organisation.
projects.overview: Established: 2007 Location: Palm Island (Bwgcolman), QLD Structure: Public company limited by shares → transitioned to 100% community-controlled (October 2021) Chair: Luella Bligh CEO: Rachel Atkinson (also Chairperson of QATSICPP) Workforce: 176 staff (as of 2026), 85% Aboriginal/Torres Strait Islander, 78% local Palm Islanders Tagline: "We tell our own stories, measure our own impact, and control our own data — community-led since 2009" 20th Anniversary: 2027

projects.title: PICC Annual Report
projects.summary: Community-controlled organisations are required to account to government funders. PICC turned this obligation into something else: a declaration that community keeps its own records, on its own terms.
projects.overview: The PICC Annual Report project is ACT's collaboration with Palm Island Community Company to build an AI-powered annual reporting system from community-owned data. Rather than hiring external consultants to write reports for government funders, PICC compiles its own impact narrative — from the data it generates, in the language it uses, reflecting the priorities it sets. The technical foundation follows the Karpathy LLM Knowledge Base pattern: PICC's 20 years of operational history, service records, and community stories are being compiled into a structured wiki. The annual report is generated from this wiki — not from a template provided by a funder.

projects.title: PICC Centre Precinct
projects.summary: A building is not community infrastructure. A community-controlled building is. The difference is who holds the keys.
projects.overview: The PICC Centre Precinct is the physical community centre on Palm Island — the hub where PICC's integrated service delivery operates. It covers fit-out, maintenance, utilities, and operational costs for the building that houses health services, family programs, employment support, and cultural activities under one roof. This is not a government building managed by a contractor. It is community infrastructure, managed by community, for community — a physical expression of the transition from state-managed settlement to 100% community-controlled organisation.

projects.title: PICC Elders Hull River Trip
projects.summary: Knowledge lives in Elders. When you bring Elders back to country, you bring the whole community's past into its present.
projects.overview: The PICC Elders Hull River Trip is a cultural programming initiative connecting Elders from Palm Island (Bwgcolman) with the Hull River area — a site of deep historical and cultural significance for the communities that were displaced and relocated to Palm Island under the Queensland government's Protection Era policies. It sits within PICC's broader Elders Group Activations: Elder-led cultural programming that brings intergenerational knowledge into active circulation rather than archive storage.

projects.title: PICC Photo Kiosk
projects.summary: 2,491 photos documented. Not by outside photographers — by community, for community, stored on community terms.
projects.overview: The PICC Photo Kiosk is a community photography storage and sharing infrastructure project — part of ACT's sovereign storytelling work on Palm Island. It provides accessible, community-controlled photo capture and storage, connected to the broader Empathy Ledger deployment and the On Country Photo Studio (ACT-PS). The kiosk sits alongside the Palm Island Photo Studio as part of ACT's infrastructure for ensuring that images of community are captured, stored, and shared on community terms — not uploaded to commercial platforms, not held by visiting photographers, not archived in government databases that communities cannot access.

projects.title: Place-Based Policy Lab
projects.summary: An evidence-based, participatory research initiative co-designing community-led policy from the ground up — where expertise lives in the community, not the think tank.
projects.overview: The Place-Based Policy Lab operates from a fundamental challenge to how policy is typically made: policy designed at a distance from the communities it affects tends to reproduce the same structural conditions that created the problems it claims to solve. The Lab inverts this — starting with community-held knowledge, using participatory research methods to surface and systematise that knowledge, and building evidence bases that communities own and can deploy. "Place-based" is the operative commitment: policy designed for a specific place, with the people of that place, grounded in the particular history, ecology, economy, and social fabric of that location. Generic policy applied universally fails communities whose needs don't fit the template.

projects.title: Quandamooka Justice and Healing Strategy
projects.summary: A justice reinvestment and community healing initiative grounded in Quandamooka Country — led by the Quandamooka people, focused on self-determination, and built on the understanding that healing and justice are inseparable.
projects.overview: The Quandamooka Justice and Healing Strategy is a place-specific, Indigenous-led response to the justice and wellbeing challenges facing the Quandamooka people of Moreton Bay and North Stradbroke Island (Minjerribah). It operates within the justice reinvestment framework — the evidence-based approach that redirects resources from incarceration toward early intervention, community support, and healing — but grounds that framework in Quandamooka knowledge, relationships, and self-determined priorities. ACT's role is supportive and facilitative. The strategy belongs to the Quandamooka community, and long-term success is defined by the community's own capacity to own and direct the work without external intermediaries.

projects.title: Redtape
projects.summary: Bureaucratic friction made visible. Art that takes the invisible labour of compliance and makes it impossible to ignore.
projects.overview: Redtape is an ACT studio art project that turns government and grant-application paperwork into a physical object — the literal red tape that the metaphor came from. The work sits in the same lineage as CONTAINED (youth detention as installation), The Confessional (institutional space made intimate), and Gold.Phone (bureaucracy as creative material) — pieces that take an everyday system most people don't see and make it stand in the room with them. The project asks the audience to feel what an ACCO has to wade through to receive funding. Not as a chart. Not as a complaint. As a thing you walk through.

projects.title: Regional Arts Fellowship
projects.summary: A fellowship for practitioners working at the intersection of art, technology, and agriculture — supporting the creative innovators regenerating regional Australia from the ground up.
projects.overview: The Regional Arts Fellowship recognises a specific and underserved kind of innovator: the artist-farmer, the technologist-land-steward, the creative practitioner whose work is inseparable from the particular landscape they inhabit. These practitioners are doing some of the most consequential regenerative work in Australia, but they sit outside the usual categories — not quite arts, not quite agtech, not quite environmental science — and so fall through the gaps of standard fellowship and funding programs. The fellowship creates dedicated support infrastructure for this work: time, resources, recognition, and connection to a wider network of peers and knowledge.

projects.title: ReSOLEution
projects.summary: A shoe design and customisation program inside youth detention that transforms young people from sneaker consumers into sneaker creators, building identity, skills, and commercial pathways.
projects.overview: ReSOLEution is a creative intervention program operating inside Bimberi Youth Justice Centre in the ACT. It gives young people in detention the opportunity to design and customise their own sneakers — working from initial concept through to finished prototype across four structured workshop sessions. The insight behind the program is simple but precise: in facilities where almost everything is stripped away and uniformity enforced, shoes remain a source of pride and personal identity for young people. ReSOLEution meets them there — not by importing an external interest, but by taking something they already care deeply about and making it a platform for creativity, skill development, and legitimate pathways to commercial opportunity. The program's name holds a double meaning: resolution (finishing, completing, deciding) and sole (the foundation of both a shoe and a person's character). Craft your future, one sole at a time.

projects.title: SMART Connect
projects.summary: A digital connection platform integrating peer support, digital access, and community connection — bringing innovation, operations, and storytelling together in one ecosystem.
projects.overview: SMART Connect is a digital platform project that sits within the broader SMART Recovery ecosystem ACT has been involved in supporting. It brings together three strands that are often siloed in recovery and community health settings: the operational infrastructure of running a program, the peer support relationships that make recovery sustainable, and the storytelling that builds community and reduces stigma. The platform is designed to close the gap between people who need peer support and the community networks that can provide it — while also addressing the digital access barriers that disproportionately affect people in recovery or experiencing disadvantage.

projects.title: SMART HCP GP Uplift
projects.summary: A healthcare provider education initiative — building GP and allied health confidence and competence in supporting patients through addiction recovery.
projects.overview: SMART HCP GP Uplift (Healthcare Provider GP Uplift) is the workforce development arm of ACT's SMART Recovery ecosystem. Where GP Kits provide practical tools for the consultation, HCP Uplift works at the level of the clinician — building the knowledge, skills, and confidence GPs and healthcare providers need to have more effective addiction support conversations. The project recognises a structural gap: healthcare providers receive limited training in addiction medicine, and even less in peer-based, non-12-step recovery models like SMART Recovery. When clinicians don't know the evidence base, don't feel confident raising the topic, or default to referral-only approaches, patients miss recovery support they could benefit from.

projects.title: SMART Recovery GP Kits
projects.summary: Practical toolkits for GPs to introduce SMART Recovery to patients in primary care settings — meeting people at the point of first contact with the health system.
projects.overview: SMART Recovery GP Kits are a healthcare integration initiative designed to bring evidence-based addiction recovery support into the primary care encounter. GPs are often the first — and sometimes only — professional contact for people experiencing addiction, yet most GP practices lack structured tools to introduce peer-based recovery pathways in a consultation. The GP Kits address this gap directly: equipping general practitioners with accessible, ready-to-use resources that open the conversation about SMART Recovery and create a pathway from the GP's office to community-based peer support.

projects.title: Staying — Country & Council
projects.summary: 📖 The flagship reflection for STAY lives at The Kettle. Read that first if you want the why in Ben's voice — the room at Oonchiumpa, Diagrama, and the four-layer infrastructure that makes the kettle legible.

projects.title: The Brave Ones
projects.summary: Real portraits. Real stories. Real young people. The ones changing the system.
projects.overview: The Brave Ones is a sustained photographic and storytelling series sitting in the ACT Studio cluster alongside CONTAINED. Where CONTAINED puts you inside the room that youth detention is, The Brave Ones puts you in front of the people who walked out the other side. It is the deliberate counter-mugshot: studio-quality B&W portraits in the dignity register that policing and media have refused to give Indigenous and system-impacted young people for two centuries. It is also the visual architecture of JusticeHub — the human face of the world model — and the answer to the photo-credit problem every justice org runs into: the entire image library for the next decade of community-led justice work in Australia, with consent built in at the layer below.

projects.title: The Caravan
projects.summary: A caravan as a venue, a dignity infrastructure prototype, and an art piece all at once. Born out of the Community Capital Leadership Retreat.
projects.overview: The Caravan is an ACT studio piece that emerged from the 10x10 Community Capital Leadership Retreat in Bowral (February 2026, see Community Capital). It sits in the lineage of Feel Good Project and Orange Sky's mobile dignity model — vehicles that turn up where the people are, instead of asking the people to come to them. But it's also an art piece in the Studio cluster sense: the caravan is a thing that carries an argument. The argument is that infrastructure for community capital — leadership retreats, peer councils, dignity services — shouldn't live in conference rooms in capital cities. It should be towable.

projects.title: The Confessional
projects.summary: A horse trailer converted into a sacred healing space — a mobile art therapy installation making mental health support accessible in remote and underserved communities.
projects.overview: The Confessional is a mobile therapeutic installation built inside a converted horse trailer. It travels to remote and underserved communities where traditional mental health infrastructure is absent or inaccessible, offering a safe, anonymous, and non-clinical space for people to engage with art as a therapeutic tool. The design is intentional: a horse trailer is familiar in rural and remote contexts, functional, and carries no clinical or institutional associations. Inside, participants engage with art-making as a route to self-expression and emotional processing — with anonymity and psychological safety as core design principles. Crisis support pathways are embedded in the experience.

projects.title: The Full Idea
projects.summary: A community-led infrastructure for youth justice in Australia. Three rings of work. Seven methods. Ten anchor communities. Three years to make it visible at scale.

projects.title: The Harvest / Witta Harvest HQ
projects.summary: A regenerative community hub in Witta, QLD — seasonal kitchen, garden centre, workshops, and venue hire on the former Green Harvest site, bringing together local produce, native plants, and hands-on learning.
projects.overview: The Harvest (also known as Witta Harvest HQ) is a regenerative community hub located in Witta, Queensland (postcode 4552), operating from the former Green Harvest site. It brings together a seasonal kitchen, a garden centre focused on native and productive plants for the Sunshine Coast, artisan workshops, and a flexible venue space — all grounded in regenerative land practice and local food culture. The physical site sits on Witta Farm, which remains in Nic's trust and is leased to ACT for retreats, R&D, and community programs. This arrangement makes The Harvest both a public-facing community business and a core piece of ACT's operational infrastructure.

projects.title: TOMNET
projects.summary: A community network dedicated to elder support — connecting older people to each other, to services, and to the social fabric that sustains wellbeing in later life.
projects.overview: TOMNET is a community network operating in the tradition of grassroots mutual aid and neighbourhood connection for older Australians. At its core, TOMNET addresses one of the most pervasive and underacknowledged health challenges in aged communities: social isolation. The network works by creating and maintaining the connective tissue of community — the informal relationships, neighbourhood check-ins, shared activities, and information pathways that formal aged care services cannot replicate and rarely attempt.

projects.title: Treacher
projects.summary: The tree is no longer in its ground. But it still carries the voice of where it came from.
projects.overview: Treacher is an art installation concept centred on an old tree pulled from the Black Cockatoo Valley farm in Witta, Queensland. The tree — removed from the land where it grew — is placed at a new site with speakers embedded in or around it, playing sounds recorded from the plot it originally inhabited. The sounds of its origin follow it. The installation's title — Treacher — is the name given to this specific tree. A treacher is also an archaic English word for one who betrays or deceives. Whether that etymology is deliberate is not confirmed in available source material. But the resonance is there: a tree displaced from Country is in some sense deceived — separated from the relationship that gave it meaning — while the installation attempts a kind of restoration. Treacher is in ideation stage. No installation has been built as of the wiki's last available source data. What is documented here is the concept, its connections, and the logic that makes it coherent within ACT's art practice.

projects.title: Uncle Allan Palm Island Art
projects.summary: A digital platform preserving and sharing Uncle Allan's paintings — works inspired by reef life and Dreaming stories — as an act of cultural sovereignty and economic empowerment for Aboriginal artists.
projects.overview: Uncle Allan Palm Island Art is a digital platform showcasing the paintings of Uncle Allan, an Aboriginal artist from Palm Island whose work draws on reef life, Dreaming stories, and the deep cultural knowledge of his community. The platform serves a dual purpose: preserving and sharing cultural knowledge in a form that reaches beyond Palm Island, and creating economic opportunity for Uncle Allan and other Aboriginal artists through visibility and sales. The project is connected to the Palm Island Community Council (PICC) and reflects ACT's commitment to cultural sovereignty — the principle that communities, not institutions, should control how their culture is represented and shared.
